cases.why: the boundary opens up: a list whose right edge lands exactly on the viewport's is treated as overflowing and flips. Nothing looks broken and nothing overflows -- the list simply jumps to the other side of its control for no reason a reader can see, on whichever width happens to produce a flush fit. An off-by-one in a placement rule is invisible in the diff and only appears on one viewport width in a hundred.

the revert is deleted, so a list wider than the room to the left of its anchor flips off the LEFT edge instead of the right. This is the fix-one-edge-by-breaking-the-other shape, and it is worse than the defect it replaces: content leaves the viewport on the side a left-to-right reader starts from, and the scroll needed to reach it goes in the direction the page does not offer.

placeList() runs one line earlier, while the list is still hidden. A [hidden] element is display:none and reports a zero rectangle, so right is 0, 0 is never greater than any viewport, and the decision is always 'as-is'. The fix is then present, unit-tested, documented and completely inert -- the same shape as the collector that was written, tested, mutation-covered and had never run.

the flip rule sets right:0 without releasing left. .lbx-list already sets left:0, so the box ends up pinned on both sides and STRETCHES from the control's left edge to its right rather than moving -- the overflow is unchanged and the list is now a different shape while open. A rule that adds a property without removing the one it replaces is the most ordinary CSS mistake there is and it survives every source read.

placeList() inlines the comparison again and stops calling lbxFlipDecision. The page behaves identically today, which is exactly the problem: the rule becomes an orphan that tests/test_listbox_edge_flip.py goes on checking in full while the page it is supposed to govern has its own copy. The next correction lands on one of the two.
